utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning and please be seated. Can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, I know that as promised, you gave me a call last -- yesterday, a little bit later in the evening. What about the next witness to come? What is the latest estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. As I conveyed to the Court last night, we are still in the process of trying to obtain the witness. There is no possibility the witness can testify tomorrow because we are even not sure the witness will be able to travel until Friday. We have not been able to contact the Victim and Witness Unit to arrange for travel because yesterday after hours, obviously they were unavailable, and we just arrived a few moments before 9.00 this morning. We will endeavour to call them at the next break and see to it that they make some arrangements if at all possible with this one witness. To the extent for the Court to know we will, of course, have and are scheduled to bring two witnesses for the following week as the Court ordered with the additional five videolink witnesses who will be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. And I only can encourage you to take the necessary action that maybe we have this witness on Friday. But in the event no later than Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just request the number of the witness so we can begin preparations in case the witness does come.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course. I thought we mentioned that yesterday. My apologies to the OTP. We believe it's Witness 001 on our 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anything else before we start with the witness? It still remains from the side of the Prosecution that Ms. Korner only wants to address the Chamber after the witness has concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may I ask the witness to be brought in. In the meantime, yesterday we had the map of Prijedor. This was S3-1. The witness marked some points on this map. Any objections to the admission into evidence of this map as S3-1?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Admitted into evidence as S3-1. Good morning, Mr. Zoran Prastalo. I hope that we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope that we finally can conclude your testimony today. I hope you had a good rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And maybe because it's your testimony, you want to come back to the one or other issue you mentioned yesterday and maybe you want to add something to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From my side, only two points: When reviewing yesterday's transcript, once again I stopped reading on page 85, line 20, when you told us that you had been invited to Dr. Stakic's father's house because there was a celebration of the patron saints, and then people are invited. And you mentioned spontaneously the family members being present and added the names. But unfortunately, you told us "and I know him well, but I can't remember his name." Is it by chance that you can now remember his name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about that. I know well his nickname, but I just didn't think about his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But when reading -- I have to confront you with the questions Judges have when reading the transcript. It's a little bit surprising that spontaneously you mentioned his -- quote: "Present was his father, his mother, his brother, his sister-in-law, Mr. Stakic." And then you continued: "His father's name is Milan, his wife's name is Bozana, and the children, neighbours were there." So spontaneously you added the name of the others. Why is it that you in the same spontaneous way added the name of the brother?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I really still don't know what his name is. I know the nickname which I told you, but it simply doesn't matter to me. I don't even know what his mother is called because there was no need for me -- I mean, perhaps I knew it and then I forgot it. It was a long time ago. And it's really not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to accept this, no doubt. You mentioned children, and you mentioned that several times you met Dr. Stakic when shooting billiards, and you mentioned that his son was present. How old was his son at that time approximately? Of course, you don't ask immediately how old are you, but approximately, 10, 20?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How often it was that you were shooting billiards together with Dr. Stakic and his son approximately? Ten years ago, 11 years ago, of course we understand that you can't give an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two, maybe three times in the son's presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A final area, I rechecked what from the point of view of the Defence would have been expected as your testimony, and there it reads - I don't know the practice that the parties have to inform the other party what is expected, and also the Judges that they can prepare. So in this what we call proffer, it reads: "The witness will testify as to Dr. Stakic's personality and character based on the fact that the witness has known Dr. Stakic professionally for several years." And then I revisited the two days' transcript and found out that for the period of time which is important for us, that is, beginning of May until September 1992, you mentioned that you visited two or three times Dr. Stakic in the building of the Municipal Assembly. But we don't really know yet what was the professional reason why you visited Dr. Stakic following an appointment via the secretary in his office in the municipal building. What did you discuss with him professionally during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I discussed about my company, its development, sought advice. Naturally, meetings, direct meetings, I've already said it, I had with the Executive Board either at their invitation or at my request. I said that Mr. Stakic, as the mayor of the municipality or the president of the assembly, could not resolve anything, but he could advise me, support me personally, or some other businessmen. And concrete matters, as I said, I solved through the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. I used to go -- during those two days of my testimony, I have told you that I went to -- I had been visiting Dr. Stakic because I could see that he was the one who was supporting private initiative in -- against others who wanted to spoil, destroy, ruin, whether out of jealousy or because we were so small, we could have overcome that. People are strange animals, and Dr. Stakic was for private initiative. Now that I'm telling you about it, perhaps it was dearer to me to meet him than when I had to argue with people from other branches of power. So he was a man of integrity. He supported the private initiative. He thought that private property was sacrosanct, and that is why I went to the doctor. And you say it was two or three. Perhaps I went three or four times. It was a long time ago because I was in the municipal hall more times, perhaps 20 or 30 times. But I'm now referring to the Executive Board to avoid any misunderstandings. When I say when I went to the municipal hall, I was in the building where there are different departments, different offices so that I would sometimes announce myself, and at times visit also the president of the assembly of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please try to understand what we can read from your testimony. Initially, you started that you had a serious problem, and you discussed it in all detail. You wanted to address the president of the Municipal Assembly, at that time, Professor Cehajic. You didn't succeed to get an appointment, but it was then the deputy on the other side of the secretary's office who made such an appointment. And you got the assistance of Dr. Stakic. So my question would be: Were there similar problems where you felt necessary to address Dr. Stakic and nobody else because you believed, as you did beforehand with Professor Cehajic that the one who could assist you would be the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go to the municipal hall to seek assistance only. There were also different meetings. I would be invited to discuss a point or other. I told you at the time when we were discussing the distribution of oil, I didn't go there to complain only. That wasn't the only reason I went there, to complain. I went because of some of my obligations. I mean, I want you to understand me. I wasn't seeking protection from Mr. Stakic. I had discussions with him because I thought that we were two individuals following the same line, sharing ideas. I hope you understand me that. At that time, I was a private entrepreneur. At that time, it was very, very tall order, very hard to be a businessman because you can be a profiteer, you can be called this or that, a speculator. You can be slapped a label on at any time. So at times I went there to see what the situation was as regards companies, work. I didn't have any particular problems, as I told you about, and had I had a major problem, perhaps I would have only asked him for advice. But it doesn't mean that I would have accepted that advice. I was glad to be able to talk with him because I thought that he understood me as opposed to some other people. He was a man -- he was a man obsessed with economy. He wanted it to really work well. Well, at times it went better, at times worse. But he fought for it. And I have it in high regard, because I did that, too, and during these two days you could see what kind of problems I had to grapple with. Perhaps I didn't explain them well enough. Perhaps they were not presented eloquently enough, but that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned on today's testimony, page 6, line 21, 22, quote: "I told you at the time when we were discussing the distribution of oil, I didn't go there to complain only." Could you please go in some more details. What did you discuss about the distribution of oil together with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying he wanted to know how things were, and I was one of the executives that he could learn it from. I was saying that vouchers were being issued, that people from neighbourhood communities were coming as had been agreed by a different decision of the Executive Board to get that oil with those vouchers or coupons or certificates or whatever you care to call them. So he wanted to know whether people were coming, whether they were taking that oil, what quantities had been supplied because that was during the Executive Board. I mean, that was a conversation in which he simply wanted to obtain accurate information about this. So it was a strictly business conversation. And I've already said that it would be -- that such discussions didn't last more than 10 minutes or something. I wouldn't even call them conferences. Those were working meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, isn't it true that you discussed with Dr. Stakic the entire problem of the necessary -- necessity to have additional oil derivatives from other countries, as you told us yesterday how difficult it was to bring -- taking into account the embargo, first to bring oil to the municipality of Prijedor, and then to distribute it in a way as regarded necessary, as it would be always in wartimes? Did you discuss these issues with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. Stakic, as far as I know - and we all know - was a physician. About oil, I put it to you, and I do it to this day, he doesn't know where I procured oil from. That is, he knew that if I had some permit to go to Serbia, then I suppose he would realise that it came from Serbia or Bulgaria. I repeat, I don't know if he knew that. But insofar as all is concerned, we never discussed oil or petrol that I was getting for the free market. So the conversation between Dr. Stakic and me was reduced to the -- to diesel needed for agriculture, just as he did not tell me whether he had any problems at his workplace which I perhaps could be aware of. And I, and let me repeat that, he never interfered with my work, and my province of work was specific. I was working professionally. But I repeat, I only discussed the supply of citizenry which was provided through the republican commodity reserves. It was a process that I explained yesterday. Everything had to be organised. And Dr. Stakic wasn't directly in charge of this. I repeat, it was the Executive Board which did that. But I say that everybody here would say -- ask whether all the people in the municipality who had been issued certificates and vouchers on the basis of cadastres of land registers, whether they were coming to get that oil, whether they were getting that oil, that is they simply was interested in agriculture, that is, the survival of people in that municipality. And my work was my work. I repeat it once again. Mr. Stakic is a man who fought - how successful he was, I do not know. But I know that he fought, and he found it difficult. I repeat it for the umpteenth time, that man had his ideas in life at that time, at that hard time, he appreciated businessmen, and I will say that it was dangerous to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do that in those times. Unfortunately, we didn't have many such individuals. There were some others who didn't have anything to do with the Municipal Assembly. There were also people in the economy from the socially-owned sector who also appreciated efforts that we were making. We were not able to help out more at that particular point in time to live, to make some money, to help those enterprises to survive. Because we always, at all times, employed 10, 15 people, they were getting their regular salaries. And that one salary could support a seven- or eight-member family which was not a mean feat. And at times, we also helped others out. So that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You emphasised the role of Dr. Stakic supporting private enterprises. Wasn't it then a big surprise that only some months later, you had to complain in writing on behalf of Hidraflex Prijedor about a decision signed by Dr. Stakic, a decision taken the 27th of August, 1992, a decision to declare property that has been abandoned state property, Official Gazette, 31st August 1992, number 3 of 1992 mentioned in your letter we provisionally marked S399B on page 2, the second paragraph? I can't understand this in the context.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain this. I have nothing against the Official Gazette or the signing of whoever had signed it. The article states that property or abandoned property rather is being expropriated or whatever it says. I have against the Official Gazette itself. But I do have a number of things against people who are trying to classify that enterprise as abandoned property. Something that is operating cannot be classified as abandoned property. If the company has a manager, then it can't be classified as abandoned. I have nothing against the Official Gazette, but probably there was property that needed to be protected in case there was property that had been abandoned by Serbian or non-Serbian population alike. I have nothing in particular against this decision that was signed, but I think I could prove that this was not abandoned property. I didn't complain about the decision. I didn't appeal the decision. I appealed the classification of our own premises, the Hidraflex premises, as abandoned property because it was never abandoned. So on the one hand, you have the Official Gazette. On the other hand, you have the Hidraflex. The Official Gazette, my struggle was to plead with someone in the municipality not to put that article there. But no, the article, the Official Gazette, I wasn't interested in those things. I considered that as normal for property to be protected, not to allow plundering, looting, and destruction of property. But our property was never abandoned. So I had this duel with Moma Vratija [phoen] who was in charge of implementing this. Someone took advantage of the situation to take over the company, but you can't take over companies which are operating and which are paying regular salaries to their employees. I think I was clear about both the Official Gazette and the Hidraflex enterprise. The Official Gazette does not only apply to the Hidraflex company, it applies to the whole of the municipal area and abandoned property therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think you can understand that I have to put the question to you. When complaining about, in this letter, about a decision published in the Official Gazette, and then there it reads, in any event, a decision signed by Dr. Stakic in August 1992. Wouldn't this be one of the occasions, as you did previously -- as you've said, vis-a-vis Professor Cehajic, that you would go immediately to Dr. Stakic and find out how come that you are signing this and giving on the other hand the impression to be the protector of the private-owned companies? And there is nothing with expropriation, and please take care that our company, Hidraflex, is not affected in a negative way by this decision. Did you contact Dr. Stakic on this issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a slight misunderstanding about the time frame we're talking, the time period. When the Official Gazette was published, this didn't only apply to my enterprise. I must say this again. It didn't apply only to my enterprise. But after Dr. Stakic's removal, the people who came to power and became members of the Executive Board, they signed my -- the decision for me. Mr. Indzic, again, I must point this out, Mr. Indzic, he may have been the president or the vice-president of the Executive Board, but he was the one who signed the decision when the decision was adopted. There was no need for me to appeal it. It was in November or in October, if I remember right. Now just for us to get this straight, when the decision was adopted, there was no need for me to talk to anyone from the municipality because I believe that it didn't apply only to our enterprise. But the whole operation began after the takeover in Prijedor. The Official Gazette was activated against our company. Whether against other companies, too, I don't know, because I had no time to think about that. I told you, all my efforts went towards the preservation of my own enterprise. So let me make this clear: There was no need for me to talk to any representatives of the Municipal Assembly because the decision was adopted then but at least it was not actually implemented then, at least not as concerns our company. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The decision is published as a decision as of 27 August 1992. No doubt, within the period of time of the indictment we have before us. But later, when making reference that this could have an impact on Hidraflex, it was a letter dated the 4th of December, 1992, making reference to concrete decision of 26 November 1992. Wasn't it at that time that Dr. Stakic was still in office as president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when the removal occurred. I wasn't interested in remembering the exact date. I must say this again: I did not address Dr. Stakic. I didn't go to Dr. Stakic because I -- well, the whole thing began in winter. And then as I said, I realised there was another struggle for me to lead, and that was through the media. So I didn't address anyone. I didn't seek anything because I had problems with people whom I have referred to already in closed session, so I made my own decision to wage my struggle through the media. And I had a number of people, a number of journalists involved. But there was obstruction against us, too, and all sorts of things, and that wasn't very pleasant. It may seem a bit strange, but I saw that things were getting serious, and I decided to adopt a different strategy for my struggle, and my choice was proven right in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, do you regard yourself as the person being primarily responsible for providing the municipality of Prijedor with oil from third countries and involved in the distribution of this oil?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Prijedor, the municipality of the assembly is in charge of those operations. The Energopetrol state-owned company was in charge of that. In Prijedor, they had their own petrol stations. In Kozarac, in Prijedor, in Novi Grad, in the Prijedor municipal territory, there were about four or five stations. In Ljubija, also, I was in charge of that station for a while. So Energopetrol, the Energopetrol company was in charge of all such operations, of all oil-related business. We only did our own work, I'm talking about my company, which concerned us. And we tried to understand other people, too. The Autotransport Company I referred to yesterday, sometimes we would wait for 10 or 15 days for them to pay, but we were no bearers of power, and we were not the key player in business either. The Hidraflex company, we were a private enterprise purely, so I do not consider myself, in answer to your question, to have been a crucial person for the supply and distribution of oil. I could have gone on without it. I could have just stayed in Prijedor. I could have just walked about the town. I could have gone to the front. I could have gone on without actually doing that job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more questions. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, yesterday you have read out parts of the document printed on the letterhead of Hidraflex enterprise. This document was signed by yourself on the 4th of December, 1992. In what capacity have you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy of the owner of a privately-owned enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Who and since what time was the owner of the Hidraflex?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain this if you like in terms of documents. As far as the documents are concerned, Mrs. Marija Popovic was officially the owner. She was the wife of Dragan Popovic. That's -- I'm talking about the documents. Formally, she was the owner but the actual owner was Mr. Dragan Popovic. I dealt with him the whole time. We made plans and we ran the company. But formally, Mrs. Marija Popovic was the owner of the company. But the actual owner, the man who ran the company, was Dragan Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Marija Popovic and Dragan Popovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marija and Dragan Popovic were both Croats. Marija was born in Stara Rijeka, near Ljubija, that's my town. And Dragan Popovic was born in Kreka. He was born there. He lived in Ljubija. After that, he had a family house in Ljubija. He had been born in Kreka because his father was a railroad worker, so they would travel around a lot just like military personnel did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And who decided that Hidraflex enterprise is abandoned property? What official body decided?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the people who same to usurp, to take away, to waste what we had preserved. The Executive Board which came into being, the one that I talked about in closed session, so you should have it in the transcript. The Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, or perhaps I should put it this way: Those people hid behind the Executive Board actually. The Executive Board was a body for them to actually hide behind. And those people who actually operated in the wings were not even members of the Executive Board, but I can give you the names of these people, the people who were behind the whole process. Mr. Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS, who got his nephew involved and appointed as a consultant to the president of the Municipal Assembly, Dusan Kurnoga. I'm only telling you the truth so we don't need to speak about this in closed session as far as I'm concerned. I think I have made myself perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You mentioned that the decision to declare property that has been abandoned state property was implemented and lots of other moveable and immoveable properties were expropriated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the decision was implemented. You know the dates. There was a lot of such property. We put together a factory, we built up a factory which was small but which was European in every sense of the word. It had all the new equipment, all the new machines, everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I'm not talking about equipment and machines. The next question: What was by and large the ethnicity of the people whose property was declared abandoned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm talking about is the Hidraflex company. Are you asking me about the Hidraflex company? Because that's all I can talk about. People there, I said, according to their ethnic backgrounds were Croats, but that's not what some people refer to it as. They grabbed at the opportunity to seize this from those people. So they didn't think about the people who were actually working there, who were running everything. As I've said before, those were extremely difficult times. Our lives, the lives of people who were working, who were still working there, were in danger because the owner and the formal owner, his wife, were in Rijeka. They were elsewhere. But our lives, the lives of the people who actually stayed behind were very much in danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I put my question in another way. Do you know examples when property that has been abandoned by the Serbs was declared state property?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: The last question: You mentioned that Dr. Stakic was a member of Nikola Pasic people's radical party. Who is Nikola Pasic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serbian writer, a politician, a writer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Contemporary writer or historic personality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can say both contemporary and an historic person. It depends very much on your point of view and how you understand these terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: He's still alive? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: He's still alive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically, no, he's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: When did he die?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prastalo. I have some different questions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Were you ever mobilised between 1991 and 1995, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995, 1996, I went for about ten days. I was mobilised. People who had a work obligation, we went towards Gradacac. I think I spent there not even ten days, but not in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Had you a work obligation during the months of May to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Which work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work that I have already described. That means, the Hidraflex company, the fuel, those were my tasks. I must say this again, I was quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay, okay. I'm quite clear about that. Another question: Where were you on April the 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And you were living in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Were you given a new identity card on or around that date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. You mean the personal identification document, the regular one, the regular ID?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Every citizen should be in possession of an ID. Now, when mine was issued, I'm afraid I really can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And you don't remember if there was a change of IDs around that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for me to know anything like that. I myself didn't need a new ID, so it just didn't matter. The only thing that -- my passport really was important for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I know. I'm not asking about that. I want to know if you were issued with a new identity card even if you don't need it, but if there was a change of identity cards by the -- around that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I didn't have to get a new ID for myself, so that may be the reason why I don't know, the reason why it didn't matter to me. The only thing that mattered was that I had a valid passport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Another question. You told us yesterday that talking about -- what you called the interrogation centres and collection centres, and I think it was page 70, line around 17, that in the interrogation centres, the persons there were questioned about weapons, arms, et cetera, or military activities or something. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've told you, I would go about the town. I would go to restaurants. I would go to the petrol station. Our people, you know what they're like. If you want to learn what's new, you go to the hairdresser or the shoe maker and you learn everything you need to know from them. Now whether the information is true, that's a different story all together. I hear a lot of things. So I simply heard about these things, people who had attacked the army and the police had been brought in for questioning. I know people were being questioned. I never went to any centre, to any interrogation centre or any of the collection centres. So I myself certainly never was there. So people were even asking me how they could reach a collection centre so that from there, they could travel somewhere else. I didn't know the procedure. I know that some people were returning home and then going back to the collection centre. But it was very confusing, and I wasn't really interested. I helped whoever I could, as I've said before. I helped a great number of people. But I never thought there was any need for me to boast about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. One last question, if you can answer that: As you heard about the interrogation centres and the collection centres, did you hear about people being beaten or killed in those interrogation centres?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I never heard about anyone being killed or beaten, escaping or returning of their own free will. But again, I wasn't interested in these things. I am a man from a different area of life. We all had a very difficult time, but I think I already answered your question yesterday when I told you where I lived, who I lived with, and who I still live with to this very day, or the people I still socialise with. Those times, the whole thing was just unimaginable for me. I couldn't believe it. I was never involved in politics myself, as I told you. I look at my questions and I think to myself, probably you think that I was some sort of an important person there but that wasn't actually the case. I waged my own struggle, and everything I achieved in life is because of my own effort. I tried to help whoever I could. All I can tell you now is I wish the whole thing never happened to begin with. Now who's fault is it, who's to blame, only time will show. In our municipality, everyone knows who caused the whole disorder or who committed the killings. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Can I ask you who caused the whole disorder or committed the killings? You say "everyone knows..."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prijedor -- I will just say a few words about Prijedor. It used to be a really peaceful town. Maybe in other parts of the republic, there was something happening. But in Prijedor, we always talked. We always talked our way through things, and we lived together. But you know what happened on the 22nd of May in Prijedor. Innocent people were killed at a checkpoint. There was an appeal for the people who had committed those atrocities to surrender. A deadline was set. 1, 3, 5 days, I can no longer remember what the deadline was. As far as I understand, and again, I was quite well travelled, and any country you come to you must stick to the rules, the internal rules of that country. Those people had actually killed soldiers and the army took several days before they reacted. That's also what happened on the Kozaracka Road I think. A young man was killed, I think, Djapo. We all know what happened in Kozarac. But who from the other nationalities, Serbs or Croats in Prijedor municipality killed anyone at a checkpoint when the situation was still peaceful, who was waiting for someone to come along and kill them, I know some of these people personally and that makes it even harder for me. One of the people who took part in the whole thing was a successful businessman, and the other person was an active-duty policeman. So he was watching over my family for 15 years. He had been on active-duty in Ljubija for 15 years, and I didn't even know who the man was, and he was providing security also for my family in a manner of speaking. I was a believer in justice. I may not be a very eloquent man. Perhaps what I'm saying seems overemotional, but I'm telling you what I feel and what actually happened. When someone attacks a soldier, you can't avoid the sort of reaction that then ensued. Those were soldiers coming back from other fronts, from eastern Slavonia and those soldiers were killed. They were ambushed and killed. The local commune Hambarine, the people who knew regardless of whether they were actually from that local commune, were requested for those -- those people surrender, and everyone promised that those people would not be touched. I'll give you the example of Gornja Ravska, predominantly a Croatian village. Why wasn't a single house attacked? Because nobody attacked the army or the police there. Donja Ljubija, take another example. All houses were in tact. All the people who had lived there prior to the event remained there to live. And in 1995, people left to head for a better life somewhere else. Eventually people returned. But everything has been preserved. So if we talk about Kozarac, I simply didn't go there because my road didn't pass through Kozarac. I passed through Banja Luka. I didn't go into Hambarine myself to have a look. But judging by what I could see from the road itself, wherever the army had been attacked, the army reacted. But this is only my opinion I'm giving you. I'm not an expert on these matters, but it is still my belief that wherever a soldier is attacked, the army will have to fight back. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be now for the Defence to put additional questions emanating from the cross-examination and from the line of questions put to the witness by the Judges. Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wouldn't have too long for redirect. I'll just try to clarify a few points. Re-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prastalo, good morning once again.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will mention the numbers of some pages and lines, but that need not worry you. It is merely for the record. Yesterday, page 41, line 9, you started telling us about what influence the president of the Municipal Assembly had on the Executive Board at the time when Mr. Cehajic was the mayor of the municipality. You said that the Executive Board was made of two, and then the Prosecutor interrupted you. Will you please tell us, what was it that the Executive Board was made of, of what two things, and why did Mr. Cehajic have influence there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I tried to explain it because I was very interested in that. I said for purely economic business reasons. So the Executive Board was made of eight members, I believe, four Serbs and four Muslims. So every time they would vote on matters, and there was a worry how could the Executive Board meet if somebody was not there because then a decision could be taken. And that is why I said that following Municipal Assembly sessions, they had major confusion in their party. And I think some were dismissed because some people voted without knowing what they were voting for. And I said that there were 41 to 45 items on the agenda, and we did not win it. And here yesterday it was very important and I tried to explain that we did not win it because Mr. Cehajic could not sign the decision to do that for seven or ten days. So the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly worked, if I may say that, by voting it, that is, they did not serve the people. And the Executive Board should be the body which leads a municipality, but they were only pursuing their only interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, did Mr. Cehajic, was Mr. Cehajic able to affect the voting officially or was his influence, the weight he pulled with four SDA members, of a more personal nature?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that he could control it, he could control, shall I say, his -- that is the members of his party in the Executive Board. So they pursued this policy which was fatal for the municipality, I mean because we know how companies worked at that time and what went on. But he had a direct say in the way his members reacted. And they enforced what they had adopted at some other meetings in some other offices that they had. I repeat once again -- I repeat once again, I will reiterate this, they were against it because they were a hundred per cent certain, a hundred per cent positive that Mr. Popovic was a Serb. And I claim this under full responsibility before this Court. However, later on, when they found out, it was laughable and it was sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 64, line 4, 64, line 18, and so on and so forth of our yesterday's record, you spoke about the participation of the police who had come to evict, that is, to remove you from the Hidraflex company.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you something, because it is important to explain to this Court how the evictions in our case take place. If somebody is allotted a flat by his company, in his company, that is a flat, an apartment which belongs to the company that has allotted him a flat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, it has been known that another employee of the company moves into that flat although he hadn't been allotted that flat. Will you please repeat the answer because it isn't in the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the company first asks the employee who had moved in unlawfully to leave the flat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the employee who had moved in -- who has moved into the flat unlawfully does not move out, then the company asks the police for its assistance to have that employee moved out from the flat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware or do you know whether the police took part in the forcible evictions in all the cases, that is, when an administrative agency decides that somebody should be evicted from a place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can give you some examples over the last years. Say, for instance, the Serb population, too, who had moved into apartments for instance in my town, and the police now go with people who reported that, that is, police is there to evict people from, say, those houses because returnees are getting back, and then these houses belong to them. It is only natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in such instances, the police is helping the ministry for refugees and displaced persons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in our legal system, it is one of the regular police tasks to assist in all cases of forcible eviction, and that is what happened in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your case when they requested that you be evicted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but our problem that that property had not been abandoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 69, line 11, the Prosecutor asks you if it is correct that the policemen of Croat or Muslim ethnicity were taken to the camp immediately after the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I gave an example. Policeman so and so, if need be I can give his name, stopped me on the 10th of May, and he was wearing a police uniform. When the incident in Hambarine happened, the man was an active policeman. So it is not true that certain policemen -- well, now, I don't know what happened in the woods, and whether all the policemen had exchanged their uniforms for guerrilla uniforms in the woods, that I do not know. But in my place, in my locality, the policemen worked regularly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat it once again. Let me give you another thing. The chief of police in my place was Croat, Branko Bijekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know until when Mr. Bijekic was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But he was a chief there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't really say. I don't know. I don't know the date. And I'd rather not go wrong there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a group of policemen took over the police station in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt after the last answer, but in counsel's question where he quoted my question, it was misquoted, and I just wanted to note that for the record. Counsel said that I had said that the policemen were arrested immediately after the takeover and taken to the camps. And that was not part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please make reference to the concrete page and line of yesterday's LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I quoted page 69, line 11. And it was part of the question about the police officers. But let the transcript speak for itself. So I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please be so kind, as we did it in the past, or at least tried it always, to quite directly from the transcript. That facilitates our work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we have to be aware that apparently you have another pagination. As for example, we have on our LiveNote, because on page 69, line 11, I can only read the answer of the witness, not the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Always the same problem, I guess, with the pagination, not with quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I think my pagination is off also, is the question that counsel is quoting where I asked the witness and you talked about -- excuse me, "that the policemen you talked about of non-Serbian Croatian and Bosnian ethnicity in Ljubija were separated after a while in the territory in Prijedor are arrested and taken to camps"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is line 3, 4, following, and it was at 14:17:56 to 14:18:24, that there is no doubt remaining. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your help, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prastalo, on page 99, there was talk about Autotransport Prijedor. Do you know if Autotransport Prijedor had its own petrol stations for their internal use?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Autotransport had in their depot, that is, in their compound, they had their petrol station. I explained it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, they don't always come to you for fuel, but only when they would run out of supply at their petrol pump?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I explained it yesterday. They took fuel from us only when they didn't have any, that is, when there would be a shortage. But they had their petrol pump, and they tanked it in at their own station, in their own compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Ljubija iron ore mine, did they also have their petrol pump within their compound?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that they were in Omarska, in Tomasica, in Ljubija, and they had their own petrol stations. But they also sometimes used our services, and that was why we existed as a company so that in case of a shortage or something, we would be there to help them out. Whether they would pay straight away or 10 or 15 days later, didn't really matter. The important thing was that we would be paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown yesterday -- I think it was Exhibit S180, and you were asked about 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the usher could show the witness this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in case 28, we have an acronym, AP Krajina. Do you know what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I explained yesterday that all those were very curious. I don't know what it means. It could be the autonomous province or it could be the auto company, that is, the secretary of the secretariat for the economy is hereby tasked for discussing at the AP Krajina level. And yesterday I explained I didn't know what it was. You asked me yesterday whether I had seen this, but I never seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, AR stood for Autonomous Region of Krajina, isn't it, and that was the acronym that was in use at the time. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in relation to this, did you have a set fuel price? For instance, did you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did have a set price. We -- our price was always lower by 15 or 10 pfennigs than at Jugopetrol pumps, that is, your prices could be set to lower level but not exceed. But we had better fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who set the prices and at what level? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the republican level. And there were regular market controls of the fiscal inspectors. One could not go above the price, but one could go below the price, and it was better for competition. If one was -- if one had some rate of return, then of course one could lower his prices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Prastalo. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution how long will it take for your questions? Is it better to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would prefer the break now. I only very few questions, but there are one or two documents I'd like to double check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Koumjian, please. Further cross-examination by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, just a few clarifications, when you talked about Autotransport and the Ljubija iron ore mines having their own fuel, would it be correct to say that nowhere in the municipality of Prijedor was there oil being pumped out of the ground or being refined, that all of the petroleum products came from outside of Prijedor, in fact, outside of the Republika Srpska and outside of the former Yugoslavia? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about -- you said that you went to see Professor Cehajic in the hope that he would have influence on the four members of the Executive Board who were of Bosniak ethnicity. When Dr. Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff and president of the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, isn't it correct that all eight members of the Executive Board were of Serbian ethnicity and chosen by the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to explain one thing. I can't answer yes or no. I think this takes a further explanation. I never begged anyone for anything. I was only asking for something that I was entitled to get. I'd file an official request, and that was the usual procedure. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because my question dealt with the makeup of the Executive Board when Dr. Stakic was president of the Municipal Assembly and president of the Crisis Staff. I'll break it down. Isn't it correct that there were eight members of the Executive Board? Yes or no, or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: During Dr. Stakic's time as the president of the assembly; is that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had seven or eight members. I can't remember exactly. I know how many there were when I waged my own struggle for my case. I know that then they had seven or eight members. I know that they had to vote and that they were outvoting each other at a certain point and that's what the whole problem was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that when Dr. Stakic was president of the Municipal Assembly and Crisis Staff, all of those members were chosen by the SDS? Do you know the answer to that? Can you answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had been appointed by the SDS. There were other Serb, in a manner of speaking, parties in parliament. I'm not sure they were all SDS members if that's what you're asking me. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a fair answer. Were all of them Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think so, though, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You talked about -- in answer to Mr. Lukic's questions this morning, you talked about evictions from apartments that belonged to the company. Is it correct that in 1992, many people's apartments, their residences, were tied to their job? They had the right to live in that place because of the job that they held?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most people got their flats from their companies, got the right to use those flats. As far as I know, there was no privatisation at that point. You couldn't purchase your flat from your company. So the company owned the flats, and then these flats would be placed at the disposal of the company's employees. So they were entitled to live there. They had a tenancy right to those flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was tied to their employment with that company. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were people also who got the socially-owned flats. So not only people who worked in a certain company, but there were many people working in a certain company who didn't get their flats from the company but rather from a socially-owned flat, from the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned today the name of a policeman from Ljubija, Branko Bjekic. Sir, are you aware that Mr. Bjekic was arrested and taken to the Omarska camp in July and transferred to the Manjaca camp on the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know that he was in my town. I've explained before, he was a police commander, something like that. He was a chief, some sort of chief in the police. I knew him well. We socialised a lot, and we played football together very often. On several occasions, I'd go home early --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to repeat the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, but the interpreter missed the last part of your answer. I'll allow you to repeat it, but just for your information I'm not asking all about your relationship with Mr. Bjekic. But if you could finish your answer but please keep in mind that we're not interested in all of your relationship with Mr. Bjekic and how you know him. But please, complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he was a police commander. I didn't know that he had been taken away. I didn't hear either that he had taken part in the incident with the army. I never heard anything like that. So if he was arrested, I don't know why he was arrested. I have no personal knowledge of that, and I didn't hear anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that your information about these investigation centres and other events in Prijedor came because Prijedor was a small town where people talked and you could even learn from the hairdresser what was going on. Did you ever ask the president of the municipality, the president of the Municipal Assembly, what was going on in Prijedor when you talked to Dr. Stakic in 1992 and subsequently? Did you ask him about the so-called investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to him about that. There was no need simply. He -- I believe that he knew as much about the investigation centres as I did, because that was within the purview, within the area of work of the army and the police. It was not up the government because they had not been the ones to set up the investigation centres or collection centres to begin with. It was the army and the police, that's as far as I understood the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic would know better than you what role he had or did not have in setting up those collection centres. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I know that these collection centres and interrogation centres were held by the army. As far as I know, the government in Prijedor, at least the way I understood the situation - don't get me wrong, it's my understanding. The government in Prijedor had no influence over the army or the police, especially the president of the Municipal Assembly would have carried no clout with the police or the army, especially not in times of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the situation was like. The police and the army were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of the witness, but before he's excused, I did refer in the cross-examination, and Your Honour referred in one of your questions, to the United Nations embargo or resolution. To the make the record of the case complete, I would ask that that be admitted into evidence, that and the European Community's resolution referring to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's first start before we conclude with this witness, we have before us a provisional exhibit, Number S399B in B/C/S only. Any objections? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but we would just ask that the Court facilitate that the translation be done in full as soon as practicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll request that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this document dated the 4th of December, 1992, a letter from Hidraflex Prijedor signed by Prastalo Zoran is admitted into evidence as S399B, and we expect the translation which would then have S399A as the exhibit number. Then let's continue with Security Council resolution 757 in the book of Yugoslavia through Documents Number 200, page 593 through 599. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S400A. Further questions by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But finally, I have to come back to one question, which I, in fact, did not understand. I can follow today's transcript, page 28, where you were asked by Defence counsel: "Do you know if Autotransport Prijedor had its own petrol stations for their internal use?" Answer: "Autotransport had in their depot, that is, in their compound, they had their petrol station. I explained it yesterday." This is absolutely in line with your testimony yesterday, but you provided, page 99, line 10, yesterday's LiveNote: "Sometimes two or three tankerfuls." And then you added that already previously, buses came to your station and were refuelled. Today you added, page 28, line 11: "And I explained it yesterday. They took fuel from us only when they didn't have any, that is, when there would be a shortage." Was there such a shortage and was -- what was the reason why Autotransport Prijedor had at that time a shortage of fuel, and how was it possible that you had additional fuel for them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were different situations. Sometimes their internal petrol station, which was within their compound, would run out of fuel or they simply didn't have the money to purchase more fuel. So they would come to me for fuel. When there was a shortage or when they didn't have enough money to buy new fuel, then they would somehow collect the money in a matter of 10 or 15 days. We would usually wait for them to pay back, and there wasn't any problem with that. But those were only two or three cases, the two cases that I've referred to. Those were the main reasons why they came to us for fuel, because they would run out of money sometimes, or they would run out of fuel, at least concerning the petrol station within their own compound which again happened whenever they didn't have the money to buy new fuel. 30.000 litres of fuel is not much, because they had many vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know the reasons why they were short of fuel at that concrete period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just tried to explain that. The Energopetrol company also had fuel, but perhaps at that time they didn't have the money to purchase it. The petrol station was open to all companies, as I've said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So your testimony is you provided better and better conditions for Autotransport Prijedor than others would have done, and you granted a credit line for Autotransport Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And as I've already mentioned in my testimony, sometimes we had lower prices for fuel in comparison to the prices that the Energopetrol petrol stations had. They had high prices sometimes. So people who ran the Autotransport company had to be sparing with their money, and that's why they would come to us, to get petrol at lower prices. And even when they didn't have money to pay, they would usually pay in 15 or 20 days. We would wait for them until they got the money to pay back. This didn't happen all the time, but on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This morning's transcript, page 28, line 15, you were asked: "And the Ljubija iron ore mine, did they also have their petrol pump within their compound?" You answered: "Yes, I believe they were in Omarska, in Tomasica, in Ljubija, and they had their own petrol stations." How did you know? Have you been there? Have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was there. My father worked for 40 years at the mines. Prior to 1990, I worked with the mines when I was working in the public sector. I was into export, and I did go around all these places. I did visit not far from my house in Ljubija, at the iron ore mines, Tomerci is the name of that area, they have another internal petrol station belonging to the mines. In Omarska, they also have an internal petrol station. And in Tomasica, I think also, but towards the end it was closed I think. But I think that there is one in Tomasica, too. I can't know for certain about Tomasica, but I think, yes, yes, there was one. The Tomasica mines had ceased to operate quite a while back. And they had problems extracting the ore, so I'm not sure about their petrol station. I think it had been closed down a long time ago. But the one in Omarska, I'm sure about that. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. You continued this morning, line 18: "But they also sometimes used our services, and that was why we existed as a company, so that in case of a shortage or something, we would be there to help them out." Did you help them out in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did, yes. They also needed oil to maintain their machinery. They had lots of machinery, and to maintain them -- they had vehicles, and they needed to switch on the engines. If the mine did not work, one still had to check the machinery, and they needed oil for that. They didn't have money to buy large quantities of oil, that is, a tank or two or three, so they would take from us a thousand litres now, now 1500 litres. And we would also wait for them to pay because we would give it to them on tick. Those were small amounts of money after all. And as they got some money, they would pay it to us. So we were not talking about large quantities of money, but we cooperated. And I cooperated, too, because I trusted those people, especially the men who ran the iron ore mine so that there were no problems with that, with giving the oil to them on tick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, in fact, you knew that the mine didn't work as such, especially Omarska, correct, in 1992, starting the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't know which part wasn't working. I simply knew that the mine was not working particularly well. And we had all grown up and lived off that mine, especially the Ljubija iron ore mine where I was born. And it was close to full -- to full operation, to full extraction. They were about to open a new pit called Vukulja [phoen]. But because of the developments in our municipality, it all came to a dead end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. The question was focussed on Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, nothing worked. Not Omarska alone, and Omarska didn't work either. People who work -- I've just explained why they took fuel from me, that is to switch the -- their engines and machinery on to check them. So all they did was maintain the machinery, and people responsible for maintaining went to work. Miners, those who extracted the ore, they didn't go to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When answering one of the questions put to you by Judge Argibay this morning, you explained that from your point of view there were reasons enough to arrest and investigate about Hambarine, Kozarac, the attempt to re-takeover of Prijedor, that this would be reason enough to take the initiative to do the necessary investigations. This was your point of view. We discussed already Keraterm. You were aware that Omarska at that time, when not being operational any longer as such, was used as an investigation centre. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it. I was never there. But I heard that Omarska and Keraterm were investigation centres and that Trnopolje was the collection centre. Now, I'm still not clear what that word means, the "collection" centre. But it is said that people came and left of their own volition there and it was easier to go -- to get out from that centre -- to get out into the world from that centre. And what you asked me about the mine, whether I was aware that it was not operational, yes, of course, I knew because my father worked there and he didn't go to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, LiveNote page 102, line 18 to 19, I asked you: "Did you ever sell fuel for the Omarska investigation centre?" And your answer was "no."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I never sold it to the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To who?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I've just said it. I listed companies, enterprises. There were a number of other private enterprises, and there were citizens, individuals. The petrol station is a public petrol station and it's in the town. So whoever came to the petrol pump of whatever ethnic origin, nobody can say that he couldn't buy the fuel he needed. On a couple of occasions, I also had to step in and if need be, I can also quote such examples when somebody was ill and...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the transcript speaks for itself. I have no further questions. Any other questions by the parties? This is not the case. This concludes your testimony. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we proceed with other issues, may I ask the Defence related to Witness 001, when did you for the first time contact the victim and witness section in order to give you any kind of assistance that this witness would be able to testify during this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, I personally did not, but we work through our case manager in that regard. And it was last week that we contacted them in connection with this particular witness, 001. And I would like to add -- I'd like to add that the -- with respect to obtaining their passports which is one of the prerequisites for them to obviously have travel arrangements made, in addition we would like to advise the Court and the OTP that we have contacted the Victim and Witness Unit, and we're in the process of securing that Witness Number 006, also be brought, so just so that the OTP has adequate notice of that. And my understanding from what they said, that they cannot come before Friday afternoon based upon what the Victim and Witness Unit has advised us. But we're still checking on that to make sure that we're clear on all the issues, Your Honour, but that's the most updated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry, but I have to go in some more details. And I ask the -- I have to ask the Defence to tell us the name of the person you contacted last week in order to have this witness as a witness for this week as ordered orally and in writing in due time once again last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll have to get back to the Court on that and ask our case manager. I don't know off the top of my head who specifically he talks to. I know some of the individuals by their first name, but for purposes of accuracy I'll, if the Court permits, get back to the Court after the lunch break with that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt we need this before we can discuss the question of sanctions for not following the orders of this Trial Chamber. Then for the transcript, it has to be added that the Prosecution is now and was since the break represented as well by senior counsel, Ms. Joanna Korner. If you so want, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say so-called leading counsel. However. Your Honour, the reason that I asked to appear before Your Honour, and indeed as Your Honour was given the message, the chief of Prosecutions was going to appear. But I should tell Your Honour, in fact, it would have been the Prosecutor who was going to appear because of the remarks that Your Honour made on Wednesday, the 5th of February of this year. Your Honour, I should add that in the light of what Your Honour said on Monday, it may be that the impression that we got which was why it was so seriously regarded that the Prosecutor herself wished to appear may have been perhaps a little misleading. But because what Your Honour actually suggested, and this -- I'm referring now to the uncorrected transcript at page 11.751, Your Honour began by saying: "In the direction of the Prosecution, we deeply deplore the approach taken by the Prosecution. From our position, it is not possible to proceed in the same way as was done in the past. And I know that the addressee of my words is not present in the courtroom." Now, can I pause there for a moment, Your Honour. It may well be that Your Honour's words at that stage were directed towards me. But it wasn't clear, and even if they were, what follows is something that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Office of the Prosecutor took very seriously at the time. "I think no Prosecutor in the entire world has the right to proceed to continue the Prosecution knowing that a person presumed innocent will, that there will be no evidence enough or that in part, incidents never will be proven and even charges can no longer be continued. To continue proceedings against a person whom the Prosecution knows that they are no longer able to proceed under the rules and not able to establish the case could amount to unfair treatment." Now, Your Honour, we read those words all of us in the office and all of us in the trial team as a suggestion that either I or the Office of the Prosecutor were deliberately and knowingly proceeding to prosecute a man that we knew to be innocent. In other words, that we could not prove the charges against him. Your Honour, that would be a slur on the professional reputation not only of myself, but also of the whole office, because it would suggest that we are not only behaving prosecutorially improperly but also immorally. Your Honour, we have taken the view having heard or read what Your Honour said on Monday that in fact that is not what Your Honour intended to suggest. But, Your Honour, if I am wrong, if we are all wrong in that, then we would be grateful to be corrected before I go any further. Because if the suggestion is that we are deliberately and improperly pursuing a Prosecution or charges that we know we cannot prove, Your Honour, that is the most serious allegation, and I know that the Prosecution would wish to deal with it. But we have taken the view that what Your Honour means, having looked at Monday, is that Your Honour is coming to a conclusion that there are, on the facts, matters that we cannot prove. But Your Honour, as I say, before I proceed, I would be grateful to be told if it is Your Honour's intention to allege the prosecutorial misconduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to refer to the same transcript you are referring to. Page 11.749. Here I said: "And a clear statement should be given in the direction of both parties. The Judges of this Trial Chamber will no longer accept a policy of obstruction as shown by both parties from the outset of this case." And these were my words, and this is my approach. Then, you should read extremely carefully, knowing better the English terms than me, that I did never say that you deliberately proceeded with a case which would lead to an obstruction of justice. Obstruction of justice, I think, is a term with a separate meaning which can amount to a crime. I just said it amounted to an unfair treatment when one -- when a Prosecution and a Prosecutor proceeds even though the Prosecution knows that in part, the one or other charge cannot be continued. And as you correctly stated, I gave one example last week. I gave it not only last week, I gave these examples from the beginning of this case. And I said that it is a fundamental problem for this Tribunal that the Prosecution charges persons from the outset in a way one could call in a cut and paste way from the Statute. All possible charges and especially the problem is all means of committing such a crime. For example, means that excluding -- that are excluding each other, you can't at the same time be the one preparing, inciting, planning a crime and at the same time being the aider and abettor of this crime. This makes the life extremely difficult for all participants in this courtroom. It makes the life extremely difficult for the Defence because they have to cover all these points, and all these means of the alleged criminal conduct.
