Our duty is to hear the case in a fair way and in the most expeditious way. We are mandated to do so by the Security Council and the Statute. One impediment is, no doubt, that the Prosecution never takes into account that it is one fundamental principle and obligation - and I know what I am speaking about - for all prosecutors to concentrate their case on the most important issues and charges. Granting jurisdiction is an extremely valuable good, and we have make use of this good in the most appropriate way. We have to be expeditious. It was from the outset, and I won't - if you invite me, I could immediately - it was from the outset that the Prosecution did not want to start hearing the case. The first reaction you can find in our decision of 22nd of March, 2002. And this approach continued and continued. And admittedly, being aware that a number of persons are waiting for their fair trial, it's the obligation for the Prosecution to concentrate on that what can be established in the most expeditious way; and in addition, to avoid a situation where the Defence has to cover an area which is unnecessarily broad and which does not allow the Trial Chamber to state, as we did on a very, very small issue, the one of whether or not it was the right of Dr. Stakic to go wherever he wanted. It is the obligation to concentrate that we are in the situation to say "these questions are no longer relevant. This witness statement is no longer relevant, and therefore, we need not hear this witness." It is impossible that a case like the case before us takes us more than one year. This would not happen in any jurisdiction of the world. Therefore, in order to protect the integrity of this Tribunal and to protect the integrity of international criminal jurisdiction, we have to take care that we speed up our cases, not to the detriment of the accused. The accused has a right to a fair trial. But this goes hand in hand with the duty of the Prosecution to streamline the case. We did this appeal several times, and I recall that we were extremely close to such a solution already in June last year. I still have the document I received from the Prosecutor herself. And she agreed that it would be correct to streamline the case and to try to come to a common solution, and it was prepared for signature for both parties. And it was the Prosecution who then withdrew that what they told us previously that they would prepare to go in some deliberations how to streamline or even to come to a common consensual solution in this case. I could give a lot of other examples. What we intend to do now is, through deliberations, to give some guidelines for the Prosecution because we are aware that the Prosecution is not prepared to act in their own initiative what they should do and what in my opinion - this is my personal opinion - they were obliged to do, taking the workload of this Tribunal as a whole, and as I mentioned before, to concentrate on the remaining issues, withdraw those points where there might be factual problems we can't overcome, and to avoid any academic exercises not necessary. It's an ordinary criminal court, and I'm acquainted that whenever there is a legal or factual problem to be solved that has no impact at all on the outcome of the case, then it's for the Chamber and for -- first of all for the Prosecution to avoid these problems. May I conclude my remarks that these remarks are based on that what I experienced when I campaigned for becoming elected judge through the General Assembly of the United Nations. I was always confronted with the question: "What can you do to shorten the case? What can you do in order to refrain from all these academic exercises in this Tribunal?" And I gave answers, and I promised that whatever will be in my hands I will do to avoid such academic exercises and to speed up the cases. And I feel committed to the promises I gave to those 118 nations voting for me and electing me as a Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I deal with a number of the points that Your Honour has made, perhaps not in the same order. But first, it is absolutely clear that what Your Honour is saying, and of course Your Honour has said certainly from very early in the case that we should elect the mode of liability, is that the Prosecution should effectively drop charges even though there may be evidence. Am I correct in what you call streamlining the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are, no doubt, different approaches. On the first level, no doubt it is where during the case, there is no longer evidence or evidence becomes doubtful based on that what we have heard during the Defence case. And please also take into account the special problems of this case emanating from the mere fact that the Judges, unfortunately, had to change during the case. But in these cases where there may be a lack of evidence, the counts or the mentioned incidents should be dropped. No doubt that also in addition, and this was what I learned 30 years ago as a Prosecutor, even if there might be sufficient evidence but for legal reasons it's difficult and additionally time-consuming, that it's appropriate to drop the one or other charge in order to come as soon as possible to the result, to a fair result, giving the expression of the may be guilt of the accused. And therefore, in fact, it's true, we can only appeal to try to convince the Prosecution that it can be appropriate and would be appropriate to drop some charges as is what is done - I know in a totally different context. But if a charge is not necessary for the outcome of the case, for the result of the case, in terms of a criminal-law case, then it's appropriate to drop these cases. And when I said we will immediately start with these deliberations, it's envisaging this goal and that we all try together to find -- to concentrate on the core questions of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Your Honour will let me address those various aspects. Then first, Your Honour, there is a difference between asking the Prosecution to drop charges which Your Honour feels are not necessary for the outcome of the case and the Prosecution proceeding on charges which they know there is no evidence to support. Your Honour, in this case, Your Honour heard full legal argument, both through the deliberations before the Rule 98 decision and in written briefs from the Defence and from the Prosecution. And Your Honours, as then constituted, the Bench as then constituted, made a ruling that there was sufficient evidence for there to be -- for the charges to proceed as laid. Now, Your Honour, the Rule 98 is very specific. It states, if I can just remind Your Honour - I'm sure Your Honour is aware of the wording - Rule 98 bis: "An accused may file a motion for the entry of judgement of acquittal on one or more offences charged in the indictment within seven days after the close of the Prosecutor's case and, in any event, prior to the presentation of the evidence by the Defence pursuant to Rule 85(A)(ii). "(B) The Trial Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal on motion of an accused or proprio motu if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." But Your Honours, the time for these motions and for Your Honours to make that sort of a ruling is at the close of the Prosecution case and before the Defence start calling its evidence. We are at present in the middle of the Defence evidence. For Your Honours to make findings of fact at this stage, which is what Your Honours would be doing, if Your Honours decide to dismiss at this stage one or more charges, Your Honours would be to do exactly what Your Honour didn't want to do before, before you've heard the evidence, all the evidence, for the Defence. So, Your Honour, our submission would be that the time is not right for any discussions of whether Your Honours find that there is at this stage of the proceedings such a doubt that Your Honours would never convict. Your Honours, that would be pre-empting completely the evidence that the Defence may call or indeed that the Prosecution may call in rebuttal. Your Honour, the stage has been passed when Your Honours, in our respectful submission, should start making findings of fact until all the -- the end of all the evidence in the case. Your Honours, the second point: Should the Prosecution, as Your Honours put it, streamline the case? In other words, drop charges on which there is evidence because Your Honours don't feel that the outcome or those -- a conviction on those charges will materially affect the case. Your Honours, the difficulty with that is it's a two-fold thing. It's a fair trial for the defendant, but it's also fairness to the persons whom the Prosecution say were victims of the actions carried out by the defendant. And, Your Honours, what may seem just streamlining to the outside world may seem as though the Prosecution and Your Honours are taking the view that, for example, because Your Honour has raised it, it doesn't add anything to this case that persons were persecuted by dismissal from their jobs purely as a result of their ethnicity, which carried with it a lack of livelihood, a lack of housing. And, Your Honours, it would be, we would submit, inappropriate to the suggest watching what is happening that that is an irrelevant matter. Your Honours, it is simply a question of the evidence being there. It doesn't add or detract from the length of this case. Your Honour, you took, as I understand it, you gave an undertaking to your electors that you would shorten trials here. Your Honour, let me assure Your Honour that although this case has been running now for something like 117 days; in actual time, it doesn't even amount to some six months. Your Honour, there are many cases in our own national jurisdictions which run for that length of time. This has been a case which has wasted no time at all and has made remarkable progress. So Your Honour is, in fact, carrying out Your Honour's promise to those who voted for you. Your Honours, in respect of the mode of liability which Your Honour is quite right, Your Honour has raised from the beginning, but Mr. Koumjian addressed when he spoke the other day, and we addressed this earlier on and throughout, it is for Your Honours to decide, having heard the evidence, we merely put the evidence before Your Honours when we called our evidence, and we cross-examined the witnesses as to effectively what we say the case is. But the mode of liability is something that Your Honours and Your Honours alone have the right to choose. So as I said to Your Honours I think some time ago, if we say our case is planning, and that is all that the Defence have to meet, having heard the evidence, you may decide, not a planner, but an aider and abettor. And we would have removed the possibility that Your Honours could find that mode of liability. Your Honour, in our submission, it doesn't add at all to the length of the case or what the Defence have to meet. We have made factual allegations against Dr. Stakic. Those are the allegations which the Defence have to meet. So Your Honours, we would submit that this is really not the time Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for Your Honours to hold these deliberations that you apparently envision at the moment. Your Honours, in respect of the difficulty which I think Your Honour is referring to of whether there are legal difficulties which may delay matters, I think Your Honour is referring to counts 7 and 8, which are the deportation and forcible transfer, if I am right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not only. There are a number of other issues, for example, related to Article 5 and the deprivation of fundamental rights which causes numerous problems and doesn't allow to take the view that additional questions are not relevant. But this would really -- it would really be necessary to go into the details charge by charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all I was going to say, and Your Honour, I've touched on what I think was Your Honour's concerns on the deprivation of human rights because I think Your Honour has dealt or mentioned it before. But, Your Honour, what I was going to say on counts 7 and 8 is this: Your Honours, there are two conflicting lines of authority at present in this Tribunal. The case of Blaskic stated that deportation encompassed effectively what we now call forced transfer. In other words, there did not have to be a crossing of a national line. However, in the cases of Krstic and Krnojelac, the opposite view was taken by the Trial Chamber or the Trial Chambers. Your Honours, there is an appeal pending at the moment in Krnojelac in which the Office of the Prosecutor has taken the position that Your Honour has; namely, that it is unnecessary to have both charges, that deportation in effect encompasses both the charges. I imagine that's a note saying I'm going too fast. But, Your Honour, the difficulty is at the moment is we cannot say which line of authority the Appeals Chamber will follow, which is why we need at this stage to leave both charges. And as Mr. Koumjian pointed out I think it was on Monday, Your Honour has heard considerable body of evidence about the transfer of persons in the most dreadful circumstances but not out of the state. Your Honour, I hope -- and may I -- this is a small point, but may I in defence of Mr. Koumjian deal with -- of all of us. Your Honour took grave exception to questions in respect of where Dr. Stakic -- why Dr. Stakic went to Belgrade. Your Honour, may I say this is standard, standard cross-examination, not only, I understand, in the common-law system but in other civil-law systems because we've discussed it in the office, that if a man knows that he is charged with a criminal offence and goes elsewhere, then it is perfectly proper for the Prosecution to inquire why at that stage he disappeared. But, Your Honour, we're abiding by Your Honours' ruling, but this would be, as I say ordinary - I was going to use the slightly unparliamentary expression "bog standard" - cross-examination in many jurisdictions, and as I say, in civil jurisdictions as I understand the matter. Your Honour, those are the points that we wish to make. But the main point I think is this: If Your Honour now starts to make findings of fact before the end of the case, Your Honour is, in fact, really going - we would respectfully submit - beyond what you the Judges as finders of fact should be doing at this stage and maybe pre-empting a considerable body of evidence that, as Your Honour said before, that one of the difficulties of Rule 98 is you didn't know what was to come, even less do Your Honours know now. And having seen the witnesses, Your Honours, our position would very much be that the Prosecution case has not lost a jot of its forcefulness. Indeed, we would submit having heard the Defence evidence that the persuasive nature of the Prosecution's case has become even more apparent. Your Honour, those are the submissions we make. Your Honours, if there is anything that you specifically wish us to address at this stage, then of course Your Honours, we will be happy to do that. But those are the submission that we, on behalf of the office, wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary to go in some of the details because I, in fact, I find some of your comments not in line and not in agreement with our decision on Rule 98 bis handed down the 31st of October, 2002. We would have to go into some more details. And it is, of course, the right for the Defence to give their submissions. Would it be appropriate for you to continue this, I think, very important discussion today, 1.30? Then, the trial stays adjourned until 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before giving the floor to the Defence for response, let me add the following remarks: A minor but important point only serving as an example for the question of relevance or not relevance is the question whether or not we can regard the question why and if Dr. Stakic took the decision to move to Belgrade is relevant for this case. First, it's undisputed that there is no crime to flee. It's no crime to flee at all. It could only be, if we would arrive at the sentencing stage, a mitigating or aggravating factor. But there is a basic principle of law that the absence of a mitigating factor can never be regarded as an aggravating factor. Mitigating factor could and would be the voluntary surrender of Dr. Stakic to The Hague. We have no evidence or any intent of this. This would be for the Defence. From the perspective of Dr. Stakic, worst-case thinking would be that he knew about the indictment and, in fact, tried to hide himself. But even if so, no inference could and can be drawn from this against Dr. Stakic. He has no duty at all to cooperate or even to surrender. Article 29 of the Statute only provides for the duty to cooperate with states. That's individual, no legal system of the world has an obligation or a duty to surrender voluntarily. Therefore, in the absence of such a duty, no negative, aggravating conclusions could be drawn from his own decision wherever he wanted to go in case we would come to the sentencing stage. Therefore, to that end, it is absolutely irrelevant which decision Dr. Stakic took outside the time frame set by the fourth amended indictment. If not conclusions can be drawn related to one of the concrete charges. It is difficult enough for this Trial Chamber to find out whether the OTP has chosen this time frame when it turns out more and more clearly that it's the Prosecutor's -- the Prosecution's case that Dr. Stakic allegedly started with the preparations of the alleged crimes already in January 1992 and continued after this time window set by the OTP in the indictment. But as promised, I do not want to reopen this debate why and to what extent the OTP delayed or tried to delay this case. We are still confronted with a motion on three documents not 65 terred and proprio motu, we asked the question why a certain document was not tendered in time, was not 65 terred, was not included when we asked for all documents to be given to the handwriting expert, Mr. ten Camp, the document of 22nd of January. We are still suffering from the absolute belated disclosure of six important statements. But let me no longer deplore the problems of the past. Let me come to the core issue: How is it possible to streamline the case? It doesn't help from my point of view, better from our point of view, we discussed this during the break, to play the ball back to the Chamber because the Prosecution is absolutely right; there is no second 98 bis decision possible. The Chamber cannot proprio motu under the current rules close the case in part. Therefore, my words, better, the words of this Trial Chamber, can only have an appellate function. Under the rules, only the OTP has the possibility to streamline a concrete case. This is why, as mentioned, since January last year, this Trial Chamber tried to convince the parties that it would be helpful to have additional deliberations how to come to the consensual end of this, and if not a consensual end of the case, at least a more expeditious end of this case as foreseen mandatorily under our Statute. Coming to our 98 bis decision, we did not - for reasons emanating from the special circumstances of the composition of this Bench - adopt or apply the standard as described by Judge Pocar in a dissenting opinion. Because from our point of view, and our -- in this case means the point of view of the Judges seized with the case before the 31st of October, we were in fact of the opinion that this rule makes only sense when the test is not to which conclusion a reasonable trier of fact could come, but for reasons of judicial economy, to which conclusions this concrete Trial Chamber could come. And no doubt, everybody could read from the 98 bis decision what would have been the outcome under this other standard. It is the submission of the Prosecution now that it wouldn't help to have deliberations on how to streamline the case at this concrete point in time. I do not agree. I do not agree because it is possible if only the parties so want to discuss legal issues and to find out where the problems are, and this would facilitate the work, if not the obligation, to exercise the obligation, by the OTP to streamline the case and to finally allow also in this Tribunal that in nearly all jurisdictions of the world is the central problem, to make use of judicial economy and not to waste time with academic exercises and to go into factual, very difficult problems which would take us months and months longer than estimated. Because one thing should be quite clear: One point is whether Defence counsel try or not try to create obstacles. The other question is the right of Dr. Stakic to have a fair trial. And this has nothing to do with concrete actions conducted by Defence counsel. And we would have to proceed even though Defence counsel believe that the case could be closed and then be later -- maybe later come and readdress the question and state maybe by other Defence counsel that the pace of the case would render the case unfair. I think we should all be aware, this is not a common-law Tribunal; this is not a civil-law Tribunal. We have a hybrid character. And it is for this that we have all -- we are all under the obligation not to find the lowest common denominator of the two legal systems, but we have to find out ways how to speed up the case. And it is for this reason that I want to distribute only as one example -- I know that the same rules more or less are applicable in most of the codes of criminal procedure in the 45 member states of the council of Europe to give you only one example. Sections 154 and 154(a) of the German code of criminal procedure, there, these are rules on insignificant secondary parities and there it reads that, "The public Prosecution office may dispense with prosecuting an offence under the following prerequisites," and then it reads, and that's the state where we are now, "If public charges have already been preferred, the Court, upon the public Prosecution Office application, may provisionally terminate the proceedings at any stage." No doubt, this can't be translated one to one in our rules on procedure and evidence. But it gives a hint. And in addition, Section 154 (a), limitation of Prosecution. It reads: "If individual separable parts of an offence or sum of several violations of law committed as a result of the same offence of not particular significance, one, for the penalty or measure or reform on prevention to be expected; or two, in addition to pertinent or measure of reform or prevention which has been imposed with binding effect upon the accused for another offence which he has to expect for another offence." Here it would be only alternative one. In those cases, Prosecution may be limited to the other parts of the offence or the other violations of law. And this, I think, is a clear hint how, in fact, we could proceed only if the Prosecution so wants. Under our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the role of the Prosecution is, no doubt, a more dominant one, and therefore, we can only invite and can't do anything else than inviting, in fact, the Prosecution to participate in these deliberations in which framework soever in order to have a more streamlined case as it is called here "Limitation of the Prosecution." May I ask that these sections of the German Code of Criminal Procedure be distributed to the parties and one, please, for the registry, as the next following J exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: J28A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that Dr. Stakic, due to the kind assistance of the booth, was able to follow this what can be read in this German Code of Criminal Procedure. But I have to emphasise, only as one example how one can proceed, and maybe one is obliged to proceed. But these are my preliminary remarks. It's now for the Defence to give their submission to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence has several comments if we are permitted to make and to address some of the statements, if you will, of the OTP. Regretfully, we only agree with the OTP in part, but disagree in many of the other aspects to it. Similarly, with all due respect to the Court, we disagree that the time or the stage for reconsideration of the evidence has passed because we're in the middle of the Defence case. Counsel for the OTP stated, and read for us Rule 98 bis again, and clearly we believe that it gives this Court the right, proprio motu to revisit those issues and make those decisions at any time. There's no rule that prohibits or no decisional authority that I've reviewed that prohibits a Chamber from dismissing counts proprio motu or allegations within a count at any time it deems that the evidence is insufficient. We would like nothing more than during the deliberation phase of this case prior to the submissions in writing and orally last year that the Court revisit those issues. We thought, much to our disappointment, that some of the issues would be resolved. All the remaining counts have stood. All the allegations both factual and legal have stood with the exception of those referenced by the Court, the instigation, and the issues where there was no evidence which the OTP has admitted with respect to any attack, destruction, or killings. We do, respectfully, invite the Court to once again look at those issues and to once again examine that which we discussed last year before the submission of our 98 bis motions, and we believe when you apply it to the rules, specifically where the Court is given the right, using the word "mandatorily shall" proprio motu make a decision on those issues. Nowhere in that section or subparagraph does it say the Trial Chamber is prohibited from addressing that or is even given a time frame when the Trial Chamber shall reach its decision on that point. To move to the next issue, if I may, the Court has touched today on page 44 of the transcript citing page 11.749 of the previous transcript Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I believe of the 5th of February, a "policy of obstruction." The Defence certainly is of the position, respectfully, Your Honour, that there has never been a policy of obstruction by the Defence attorneys, by Dr. Stakic, or any members of our team at any time. Our intent has never been to obstruct the process or to delay the process from reaching the final decision in obtaining a fair trial for Dr. Stakic. Similarly, I may add, although we have disagreed on many, many points with the OTP, we have never alleged that there was a deliberate or intentional obstruction or frustration of the case as it relates to Dr. Stakic. We do continue to insist on previously filed written and oral submissions, although denied, that the OTP has in possession and has had in possession documents which we continue to maintain are exculpatory. By my comments, we are not waiving our position on those prior pleadings, motions, and oral submissions. Nevertheless, we are troubled professionally and personally that there's at least -- at the very least a thought of this "policy of obstruction." We would like to visit with the Court at any time and at your convenience the history of the efforts by the OTP and would like that opportunity to submit it in writing if necessary. If I may turn to the next issue. The Court is correct when you mention the word "cut and paste" of an indictment. Interestingly enough, the OTP's, in my view, policy and practice has been just that, to cut and paste. Doesn't matter who the defendant is; who the accused is; or where in the former Yugoslavia that accused was located, or what the actions or conduct against that accused have been. Although I have not read every closing argument that the OTP has given in this Tribunal, I dare say that the same argument offered today by Ms. Joanna Korner that in fact as a result of the Defence witnesses, their case is enhanced or it somehow has been strengthened. That's the same cut and paste argument that they use in every single case that they ever present in this Tribunal. We would like to think that these cases are individual, that these cases are separate, that these cases are distinct from one another. The OTP, however, maintains their policy of cut and paste. If we only look at Mrs. Biljana Plavsic's indictment, simply transfer the name, and we'll find the same eight counts with the same factual allegations, planning, ordering, instigating, and/or otherwise aiding and abetting, for every defendant, for every accused, they make those allegations. I agree with the Court and I agree with the OTP that the Court has requested of them at the outset of this case, if not prior, to select and elect their mode of liability that they wish to charge our client. They have not done it at the outset of the case. They have not done it during the 98 bis stage of the case. And they won't do it at the end of the case for one simple reason, in our view. And I recognise this is not an oral agreement on our final submissions, but the reasons they cannot select the mode of liability or culpability is because they don't know themselves and have no confidence in which mode may or may not convince three professional Judges. And the reason they don't know and don't have that confidence, we submit, is because there is a lack of evidence. So instead of standing strong and steadfast on the rules and the facts that they have, they have chosen instead to throw everything and anything at their disposal in front of us and have someone else make that decision if at all possible. We think the deliberations and that stage of the proceedings would be effective and be most helpful, as we thought during the 98 bis stage. However, having read the decision on 98 bis, with all due respect to the Court, we do have some difficulty in understanding perhaps some of the representations or arguments that were made at that time. Now, let me address an issue that the Court raised, although a minor point and now seemingly so irrelevant. The Defence would not necessarily object to the issue of whether Dr. Stakic fled or didn't flee. But when the OTP asked the question, they are asking it for aggravation. But the fair question, because they are, as we are, officers of the Court, and they are the protectors of the people, the fair question would be -- instead of asking whether Dr. Stakic, being such an honourable and noble man, would he have run away from an indictment? They should set the proper question, and we can all look on our computers today and find that the indictment for Dr. Stakic was secret, confidential, not disclosed to anyone including Dr. Stakic, and only was issued public days before his arrest and his incarceration. That's a fair question. Who would run if he didn't know he was under indictment? I understand it's an irrelevant point. For the Defence, it's not. And the reason it's not irrelevant is because it's the truth. And it's our obligation to bring forth that truthful evidence. We recognise the Court's ruling. We will abide by it. However, we're still troubled that although a minor point and only used as an example, it seems to raise its head time and time again. Similarly, the OTP has made other minor allegations such as whether someone gave a eulogy at a funeral. The evidence they produce is inconsistent clearly with the documents they submit although a secondary and tertiary level hearsay of the document. It's not in the indictment. It's not a crime to eulogise someone. However, the case has taken a turn, and the OTP has decided instead of bringing forth their strongest case, to try to muddy the waters, if you will, with evidence that is irrelevant and immaterial and has no basis in fact or in law. The next issue we would like to address, and that is the OTP's view of why they purportedly cannot select a mode of liability or culpability and why they cannot elect to drop charges. I submit to the OTP respectfully that the honourable and respectful people of Bosnia and specifically of Prijedor would only need to listen to the testimony given by the witnesses such as the most respectful Dr. Minka Cehajic and how she described Dr. Stakic and how their witnesses described his personality, his reputation, and his characteristics. It is those witnesses, as well as the witnesses brought forth by the Defence, that can shape the thinking of not only what Dr. Stakic's intent was for all eight of the counts in the fourth amended indictment, but it is also necessary, we submit, that the OTP revisit both in their conscience and in their heart that those statements given by individuals who were also party leaders of the SDA, whether they themselves have ever utilised or used the word that Dr. Stakic was discriminatory in his intent at any time. Instead, we submit, and the record is clear, we have highlighted in our 98 bis motion, the Court has in part, we believe, necessitated by the rules, and also including it in a footnote in their 98 bis order highlighted some of those specific actions and conducts relating to intent of Dr. Stakic. The good news for the OTP is that I agree with their comment that they gave on page 50 where they submit, on line 23: "This has been a case which has wasted no time at all and has made remarkable progress." I submit to the Court, despite the past practices of other trials and other Chambers, this case has not been unduly delayed or unnecessarily stalled by virtue of either party. There have been hiccups, and there have been bumps on the road for both sides. Our defence is not to suggest that our recent issues and problems with witnesses, the fact that the OTP experienced similar problems or issues. We only submit that to the Court so that the Court, when viewing the totality of the circumstances in this case, we believe that it will find that the Defence, indeed, has acted expeditiously and in good faith at all times. We regret, as does the Court, and I'm sure the staff that's present here today and otherwise assisting the Chamber, that there have been these delays. It is unfortunate, and we regret that not only for the Trial Chamber, the OTP, the staff, but also for Dr. Stakic. It has been difficult at times for him to sit long periods of time here in the courtroom. As he shared with me recently this week, he was brought to the courthouse, I believe, on Monday at 20 to 8.00, and then he left at approximately 5.30, arriving in the Detention Unit somewhere between 6.00 and 6.15. He continues to maintain and continues to insist upon us, as the Court does, to reach a conclusion in this case as soon as possible and as soon as practicable. However, we will not, and we cannot, under our duties as officers of the Court rush a case and present evidence unless first the Defence and its attorneys are fully satisfied that we will bring forth this witness, and until the Defence is satisfied that it is a witness that is not only relevant but necessary for the allegations in the indictment. We are endeavouring to meet those needs on a daily and regular basis. We believe in good faith we are accomplishing that goal. We believe, as we've stated on numerous occasions, this case will end as the Court has ordered on the 21st of March. We recognise that's the Court's order. But we also believe and insist that the case ends at that time. To address another point that the OTP has raised, on page 51 of today's transcript, this morning's transcript, they state commencing on line 14: "We have made factual allegations against Dr. Stakic. Those are the allegations which the Defence have to meet." Those factual allegations is exactly what the Court has discussed with us, I dare say ad nauseum, but on numerous occasions. Can we indict and charge a person, an individual, whether they take this issue hypothetically, theoretically, or specifically in any case, with alternative theories or inconsistent theories such as planning, ordering, instigating, influencing, and then claiming he was otherwise aiding and abetting? Make the decision. The Defence would curb their witnesses based on that decision. We would curb the remaining witnesses based upon that decision. But it's our obligation to fulfill each and every one of those factual allegations, not legal, but factual allegations that they have asserted which in our view are baseless and without merit. I dare say that we can anticipate the arguments of the OTP in their final closing argument, and I would suggest to them that they merely submit that argument so that we can streamline the case pursuant to Rule 92 bis of other cases, and merely just have the Court transform the name of the defendant or the accused. They have not come up with a novel idea in our view. They have not come up with a specific factual allegation other than hearsay, double and triple hearsay, to attempt to have any charges against Dr. Stakic stand. The Court has now, for I believe at least the second time, cited the German Statute and German decisional authority. We likewise invite the Court to examine the decisional authority of other nations as well as the German decisional authority on the weight and character of hearsay evidence in criminal proceedings. It is unique to this Tribunal. The Court has specifically made reference of hearsay when a Defence witness was on the stand and asked him respectfully to share with us his personal knowledge and not that which he has heard from others. We applaud that view. We incorporate that view. We wish that principle would be applied not only for the Defence case, but for the OTP case and other cases as well. In closing, when we address issues which are our duty, such as mitigation or aggravation, the Defence without specific guidance from the Court cannot and, I dare say, will not speculate on what evidence we shall, should, or could have produced. We will with all the powers that we have present all the evidence which may give any inclination to alleviate both the issues of liability and culpability as well as sentencing. That is our duty, and that is what we will continue to fulfill. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I expect final remarks whether or not -- or remarks in response and then remarks to the question whether or not it is from the point of view of the OTP helpful to start a phase of deliberation, I only want to express my disagreement with the view taken by the OTP to that end. It was the Prosecution stating in the 98 bis motion that the Trial Chamber can only proceed with concrete charges on the basis of the evidence introduced to date. We endorsed this view. We said in conclusion, the case can only worsen for the accused, that the degree of the responsibility within a concrete maintained charge or in relation to a factual allegation as well as with regard to mitigating or aggravating factors may change on the basis of additional evidence under Rule 85 and 98. Once again, a problem with this hybrid character of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. But I think there is no point waiting maybe for additional witnesses called by the Defence and giving by chance, not deliberately, additional evidence in favour of the Prosecution. I think when we respect the decision that we have to work in principle under these rules providing for a separate Prosecution case, a separate Defence case, and then maybe even a separate Judges' case. But when we have agreed on this, then we can't wait. And I think it's important in all cases and under all legal systems that had you on a day-by-day basis decide what can be done in order to be more expeditious, and we shouldn't give up our hope that is possible, and we are under the daily obligation to find out whether, in fact - in the moment, this is not a concrete question - whether or not the deprivation of liberty is still justified. But to be quite concrete, in the moment, the question before us is: What can we do in order, as I said, not to come to the lowest common denominator, but to bring together the advantageous parts of both legal systems in order to come to better solutions not only for this case but also for cases in the future. But no doubt, it's the right now for the Prosecution to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I respond to that last aspect first. This is neither a common-law nor a civil system, as Your Honour has remarked on a number of occasions. This is a system that is bound by its own Statute and its own rules. And, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect to Mr. Ostojic, that rule makes it absolutely clear in respect of submissions of no case to answer to be made within seven days of the conclusion of the Prosecution case. And as Your Honour has rightly said, it isn't a matter for Your Honour reopening it. It's a matter -- Your Honour, effectively, it comes down to this: Your Honour would like us to drop charges. When all is said and done, that's what it has to be because as Your Honour has also pointed out, the Statute makes it absolutely clear it's the Prosecutor who decides what charges to bring and what shall go on the indictment as obviously overseen Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by the confirming Judge who has a look at the charges that are on the indictment. Your Honour, there are really two things. Your Honour has said or the Bench said there was sufficient evidence at the Rule 98 bis stage. Your Honours now would either have to be saying by these form of deliberations, we made an error, and we wish to correct the error that we made, in which case, Your Honours, we would be certainly asking for time to make further submissions on the matter. Or alternatively, Your Honours could indicate where academically speaking it is the view of the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution might consider withdrawing some of the present charges or factual allegations within the charge. Because with the greatest of respect, if it's not academic, then Your Honours are saying "you have reached a decision at this incomplete stage of the evidence that there is insufficient evidence for you to convict." Your Honours, to do that would show that - and I say this respectfully - Your Honours weren't prepared to listen to the rest of the evidence with an open mind. And, Your Honour, that would be most unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, this can't stay on the transcript without immediate answer. What I said was only the case can't worsen during the Defence case. During the Defence case, it only can turn to the better and be of advantage for Dr. Stakic. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, I'm sorry, that's simply not right. The case very often gets worse for the Defence during the Defence case. The Defence put on what they hope will assist their case. Your Honour, in reality, I mean, I would say in 80 per cent of the cases, it's a truism, the high point of the Defence case is sometimes said to be at the Prosecution -- at the end of the Prosecution evidence. Very often with the Defence case, it gets worse for the Defence. It's not what they intend, but that's what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think I addressed this point quite clearly. I made reference to maybe even in a cut and paste way, we did it from your arguments under 98 bis, that the Trial Chamber can only proceed with concrete charges on the base of evidence introduced to date. And what about the worsening of the case? It's quite clear, and it has been ruled and we are no longer seized with the 98 bis decision. Please accept our decision. You can read it on page 4, the last sentence of our 98 bis decision. And this is a decision of our Chamber, and this is endorsed also by the Judges sitting now here in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's a misunderstanding. I'm sorry. Your Honours, we made it absolutely clear because we wanted to ensure that at that stage, Your Honours took into account only the evidence that had been led by the Prosecution. You could not take into account, we submitted and you agreed, any evidence that might come, that might affect the decision. But we're looking, Your Honours, now, at a completely different scenario, which is having got through that stage, come the end of the evidence, you look at the evidence as a whole. You don't divide it in our submission into Prosecution evidence and what the Defence led; you say: "What is the evidence in this case? Either we are satisfied so that we are sure that the defendant is guilty of the particular offence, taking all the evidence including that led by the Defence, or alternatively, we are not satisfied at the end of the day having heard all the evidence that the test has been established," which is a different test from that at half time. You the Judges have to be sure. So, Your Honour, our concern is this: And I repeat again, Your Honour, that this is not, we submit, the stage at which Your Honours can do anything other than perhaps academically as I say suggest to the Office of the Prosecutor that there are certain matters which perhaps they might like to reconsider. But Your Honours, anything other than that, and we will be -- the problem is it will have the opposite effect, I think of what Your Honour intends. It's not going to shorten matters because we will be seeking time to look through the evidence to readdress Your Honour again on those matters. Your Honour, if Your Honours want to do that without suggesting in any way that you've come to any sort of decision on any of the legal charges and the facts relating to them, then, of course, Your Honours are perfectly entitled as you call to give a judicial hint. And we will, of course, consider the matter. But anything other than that, Your Honours, we would submit is inappropriate at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Your Honour, if I may. I think, respectfully, to my learned friend that the OTP's obligation is set forth rather clearly and the rules are rather clear. The OTP knows and does not believe in the principle, fundamental as it may be, of the presumption of innocence. They state to the Court on page 71, line 1 just moments ago: "What is the evidence in this case? Either we - and I won't dare speculate as to who they are referring to as to the we - either we are satisfied so that we are sure that the defendant is guilty of the particular offence..." I submit to the Court that that is not the standard of review either at the beginning of the case, at the stage of the 98 bis pleadings, or at the conclusion of the case. This Trial Chamber has not, and it is not their mandate, I say most respectfully, to determine or to be sure that an accused or a defendant is guilty. Although hesitant and confident that this Trial Chamber knows its duties and what the burden of proof is and whose responsibility that burden of proof falls upon, it is not this Trial Chamber's duty to make sure that there is enough evidence so that an accused is found guilty or to be certain. Your evidence or your task, I should say, is to examine the evidence in an objective manner and to weigh the testimony of the witnesses, to weigh the testimony of the documents, to weigh each and every one of those individually and collectively on each and every allegation, both factual and legal, on each and every count. The OTP may be right in the respect, although I'm not sure why they fear it, but they may be right that decisions have been made or there's some predetermination. But as we know, all of us in this courtroom and in this Tribunal as professionals, we most certainly have predetermined views, and we certainly have our views shaped and changed at times by the ongoing process of a trial. We are confident the Court, each and every one of you, has not made a decision on any of the counts in the fourth amended indictment. A decision of guilt at this time would most certainly not only be premature, but it would be, in our view, a violation of the very mandate and rules prescribed in this Tribunal. However, the Trial Chamber has received in total the evidence of the OTP, and it can, we submit, at any time by the powers given to you by the rules, not only through judicial hints but specifically through orders to try to streamline a particular charge, to dismiss a specific count or counts, and to streamline the case in its entirety. We invite the Court to do that. We urge the Court to do that. One last point, if I may, I was in the response by the OTP hoping we would get a breath of freshness instead of the same cut and paste that it's a truism. The reality, not the truism, is that the OTP respectfully in their narrow view of the facts and narrow view of the evidence would never dig deep in their conscience and in their heart and say that any charge or any fact should be dismissed. The truism or reality is that this Court gave specific, concrete, elaborate judicial hints. If we take those comments by the Court and apply them to what it is specifically that the OTP decided to drop or discharge, we cannot accept their comments now or at any time that they will examine the Court's view, duly consider it, and possibly, always giving that little shed of hope, possibly decide to drop or dismiss factual allegations, counts, or legal arguments. It will never happen. It has never happened. Because their truism is and their mandate is to throw everything against the defendant and hope through the masses of documents and testimony something or anything would stick. We ask this Court to reject that prior, current, and apparently futuristic position of the OTP. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can I can't see any request for taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could take a few minutes of the Court's time, just one response briefly on the matter of dropping incidents. We did try to streamline the case. It's not that we threw everything against the wall. There was, for example, a minor -- well, it wasn't minor to the people involved, a massacre in the village of Jaskici that was found in the Tadic decision. The witnesses who testified taking the judicial hint that enough crimes had been proven, we dropped that rather than attempting to 92 bis that or litigate the adjudicated facts from the Tadic decision. And also, I would just like to briefly address this issue of why we put on evidence or asked witnesses about Dr. Stakic's going to Belgrade. We accept the Court's ruling, and we have since the Court indicated its feelings, have not pursued that. But because the allegation seems to be that it was misconduct on the part of Prosecution, we would just like to talk about it because it's perhaps a difference in legal systems. Mr. Ostojic is familiar with it from sharing the same jurisdiction that I do. It is not offered as evidence of aggravation. No one's saying that flight is a crime. It is offered, and I present the jury instructions that we have in my jurisdiction, as indirect evidence of consciousness of guilt. The fact that a person doesn't know about a formal indictment only increases the relevance of a person fleeing a jurisdiction in order to -- showing that they are conscious of the crime and their own responsibility. I think the most memorable case I did before here was the rape and murder of a 3-year-old girl. The principal evidence we had was that the accused person had fled Los Angeles in the United States the day that girl's body was found in his apartment. That's just common sense that a person who suddenly leaves, in this case the position of president of the municipality, to go to a country where there is no chance of him being arrested. It was our view not -- we thought it was certainly ethical to put on that evidence. In my system and Mr. Ostojic's system, I understand from talking to another lawyer who's from a continental country, in that particular country that that evidence would be allowed. But we accept -- don't think we need it. We accept Your Honours' ruling, and we will no longer pursue. But I just wanted to explain why we presented it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you for this additional comment. I think it's helpful to that end that, in fact, we have to live with different approaches and something -- maybe we feel that it's mandatory, but to that end, as you mentioned right now, I think the continental European approach, and I know what I'm saying having taught this in several countries in transition, especially in middle and eastern Europe, that you cannot draw any inferences from the fact that worse-case thinking - Dr. Stakic, please don't misunderstand this - that in fact if a person decided not to surrender or even to flee, there may be sound reasons for doing so, and therefore, even from a human rights perspective, it's not allowed to draw any inferences. But we have to live with these different views, and we have to overcome these difficulties. We are mandated to overcome these difficulties. And therefore, we saw it as our obligation to openly address that what we regard as obstacle for a more expeditious procedure. And it was on purpose that at the same time, we addressed both parties because when discussing, and we are discussing day by day the ongoing case, that we came to the conclusion that there is, in fact, something wrong. And no doubt, also the Trial Chamber, as such, has contributed when being not rigid and not strict enough vis-a-vis one or other witness in the past and allowing questions being not relevant in order to avoid long discussions on the relevance, we have to come to some solutions. And I understand that the Prosecution prefers not to have deliberations at this point in time instead of this -- the method of giving judicial hints. But please be assured that the necessary judicial self-restraint limits our possibilities because the one or other party to whom it may concern may draw wrong inferences from any judicial hints to that end that maybe we have already found a decision against the Prosecution or against Dr. Stakic. So therefore, for us, it's extremely difficult. It's easier for the Prosecution, if the Prosecution is not prepared to act proprio motu in this case, then there is no discretion for the Trial Chamber. And here, I am in full agreement with that what has been said by Ms. Joanna Korner. There is no second Rule 98 bis possible. It's only within seven days after the close of the Prosecutor's case. So for the moment, there is no additional possibility. I can tell you that this is the most-discussed issue in the bureau, and we will continue with this that we change as soon as possible the rules in order to streamline the cases to that what is really necessary for the purpose of a criminal law case. And let's try to proceed this way. And this is true in both directions. We are not prepared to continue on a day-by-day basis fighting for documents, fighting for proffers coming one hour earlier or later. We have set strict rules for the proffers, for the rules to apply in preparation of a witness, and I hope that we shall overcome the next weeks. And no doubt, this case will not end before Dr. Stakic has had the opportunity to hear the witnesses that are relevant and important for his case. We set the deadline, 21st of January -- of March, sorry. But in case that there should be any delay caused by one of the parties, it would be necessary to proceed with this case, and this would have an absolute detrimental impact on other cases - and I don't want to discuss it any longer. The parties know very well what I'm speaking about. This brings me to the next question. I asked the Defence, in order to try to find out how we can assist you, whom did you contact in the victim and witnesses section, at what time for the first time that you would need witness or you want to call Witness 001.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. The Defence has worked with the liaison of the Victim and Witness Unit, and we have spoken and corresponded through e-mail with their representatives whose name is Isabel Skukan. I apologise to her. I just want to add one thing if I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. may, it seems that - and the Defence would like to invite the Court to visit this issue in detail with us - however the Victim and Witness Unit has been enormously helpful and has been with each and every one of our witnesses always there for them, and our witnesses have specifically stated that they are kind, attentive, pleasant, and most helpful in providing them with the needs that they require, both the accommodations, the pickups, both here and abroad. Our complications arise, Your Honours, from the limited time that the witnesses have to get passports and visas issued. The governments from my understanding do not give them open-ended travel and limit it by days. The Victim and Witness Unit does not coordinate the passport and visas for the witnesses. That's done at the place of residence of the individuals. That process last week was, unfortunately, frustrated because there was a holiday on both Thursday and Friday where it's our understanding that the governmental and administrative offices were closed down. We have for Witness Number 65 ter 006 the visa and we have made the application for him to be present. The Victim and Witness Unit has been most cooperative in trying to secure that that be brought on Friday. That does present a problem for the Defence because we would like to meet with this witness. It also presents a problem -- he just has a passport. We're still waiting for him to get the visa. It's a process that is time consuming. It's also presents a problem for the OTP and the Court because we can't give you the proffers in advance because we still don't specifically, other than what was submitted previously to the Court I believe on the 18th of November of 2002, what it is that they are going to testify so that we could share it all the parties. We would request that those two witnesses, as ordered yesterday, and we're giving the Court the number, 001 and 006, be the two additional witnesses for next week with the five videolink witness that we have. Also, if I may, with all due respect, although we asked this on a couple of occasions, and we were granted this by the Court, we need and would like an opportunity since the case is coming to a close, or nearing a close, the opportunity to meet with our client, Dr. Stakic, more than we have in the past. For two reasons: One, we would like his evaluation and his assessment of the evidence so that it can be incorporated both in our oral and written submissions, but also, two critical witnesses among others, namely the experts, will be called in the last ten days of the trial. We most definitely believe we would need his participation, and we would like to inform him at the very least of what the documents and the reports state. Once again, we apologise to the Court very sincerely, to the OTP, to the staff, the interpreters, and all those involved because of this unpredicted delay in bringing witnesses this week. We were misguided, and our interpretation of the Court's order or notice for two judicial witnesses, we misread it. We're not suggesting the Court was not clear in that order. We were under the opinion and impression, since the Court has the power to have witnesses come when it calls them, and probably can expedite visas and passports to witnesses, we felt that this week, in addition to the witnesses and witness that we had, those two judicial witnesses would be called. Again, we assessed the situation, Your Honours, that if a layperson or a character witness would take somewhere in the neighbourhood of a day to a half a day to conclude his testimony, certainly the two witnesses that the Court has called because of their involvement in all the aspects of the fourth amended complaint would take no less than a day and a half each. In fact, I dare say that we can conclude each of them within three days. That was our mistake. We apologise for that mistake. We can reassure the Trial Chamber that if there are any other speculative reasonings or rationale on the Defence part or uncertainty as to what the orders are or were, we will contact the Court immediately and ask for clarification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also to be quite clear on this point, as you already indicated, I think the order couldn't have been more clear. But it was the Defence itself making the submission that it was not possible for them to bring these two witnesses or call these witnesses to The Hague, and no doubt, a court order alone, also taking into account at the time necessary, does not say that the requested country and the persons will, in fact, appear in the envisaged time frame. We discussed it, and it's reflected on the transcript, that it might be necessary to subpoena these witnesses. And until today, we really don't know whether, in fact, they are prepared to come to this Tribunal. Therefore, we can't give you any other hints. But no doubt, the Defence was all the time, and you admitted this and you apologized and we accept this, under the ongoing obligation to call witnesses for this week. But I have to emphasise that it was already last week Wednesday that we discussed it and we informed the Prosecution on this issue, that we asked Defence counsel at least to take care that witnesses should be present on Thursday and Friday and immediately to contact the Victim and Witness Unit last week Wednesday. And there was no holiday here last week Wednesday. Or the possibilities were for the Defence to try to do the necessary related to the Victim and Witness Unit. And unfortunately, I was informed by the Victim and Witness Unit that only this morning, for the first time, the Defence contacted the Victim and Witness Unit on Witness 001. And therefore, our request to have a clarification and that we avoid all these rumours, that we have a clarification and that this should not trouble the atmosphere additionally in the courtroom. So please, make sure that you can - and here, I think the burden of proof is with the Defence - that you in fact contacted already last week the Victim and Witness Unit in order to have available these witnesses. I need not emphasise once again that it's a question of some thousands of dollars per day that have to be spent whether we hear a case or the courtroom stays empty. And therefore, there's a huge responsibility on all of our shoulders. After the break, I have to ask the Prosecution to comment on the question of the belated presentation of the one document of January 1992 before we can hand down our decision on the request of the motion of the Defence related to three other documents where the Defence complains that these documents have not been 65 terred. Then we expect an answer or a response - I take it as the right to be heard - to the question whether or not the acts conducted by the Defence during the last days, especially the last motions are adequate or whether it seems from the point of view of the Prosecution necessary to sanction this what we might see or assess as a not adequate way of continuing with the case. You know about what motions I'm speaking, especially the one we discussed yesterday in addition. Then we will proceed after the break with the reading out of the documents tendered by the Defence last Friday. We had no time at that point in time to have them read out by the witness. The Defence has already submitted they do not want, and they do not feel it necessary, that the witness comes a second time. We appreciate this. But we have to assess what is included in these documents we have available in B/C/S only now. I would kindly Madam Registrar to check during the break what is the most appropriate way to have these documents read out in the courtroom, that there are three options. First, that's it read out from the booth extremely slowly; that it's read out in the courtroom in open session or, in order to protect the members of the interpretation unit, that we read it out in closed session. These three options are free. But we have to do this today. And during the break, the Trial Chamber will decide based on the submissions by the parties, which are not consensual ones, whether we proceed with deliberations tomorrow or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour breaks, there's just one matter I need to raise after the break as well. But can I just ask, did Your Honours see a copy of the Prosecution submission into Trial Chamber I in respect of Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask in return, did you receive the document sent to our Trial Chamber that Defence counsel of Ms. Plavsic said they would not be prepared that Ms. Plavsic will testify in this case not before the sentencing judgement in the other Trial Chamber has been handed down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apparently, we did. But, Your Honour, there is a matter that arises out of this whole scenario, which -- if I could raise after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's, no doubt, necessary because the case, of course, does not end the 21st of March. We have rejoinder. We have rebuttal. We have rejoinder. We have closing arguments. And there is a likelihood that the judgement in the other case will be handed down before we come to the closing arguments in this case in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not quite the matter I want to raise. But if I know that Your Honours have seen what was said by the Office of the Prosecutor in her case, well that may assist because it does affect some actions that we have to take. So I would like to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. We all should be prepared to discuss this issue as well after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we could only be given a copy of that submission in Courtroom Number I. We did not receive it. So we would be grateful if we could get that copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It should be distributed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can provide the Defence with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start, I have the impression the ventilation system doesn't function as usual today. It's extremely warm in this room. Maybe there could be somebody of assistance. Thank you. Following our deliberations during the break, the Trial Chamber has decided that based on the submissions given by the Prosecution, it makes no sense to enter into new deliberations or discussing legal issues. This would only make sense if both parties would be prepared in the same way really to discuss these legal questions in open court. For the same reasons, the Trial Chamber will refrain from giving any judicial hints in the future. I think there were not judicial but hints enough in the submissions by the parties alerting this Trial Chamber that we have to show even more self-restraint than in the past in order not to endanger this case. We deplore this development, but we can't see any alternative. Let us now turn to the next point. During the break, we learned that it would take a longer period of time, and it would not be possible until 4.30 to read out the documents, and it's easy to understand that the interpreters need time for preparation, that these documents are read out. Therefore, they will be read out only tomorrow morning starting 9.00. The next question is, once again, and finally: What about the witnesses to come? We learned today that even today, both envisaged witnesses do not have a visa. Therefore, it seems to be doubtful whether they can arrive on Friday, on Monday. If you could give us some better information, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is the first, Your Honour, we hear that it's doubtful whether they can arrive on Friday or Monday. We're under the impression that at the very least, 006 is able to arrive late Friday or Friday afternoon as the case may be. So we expect them if not to be here Friday they will be here Saturday, and they will be, as ordered by the Court, available to proceed next week. But we will double check that and get back to the Court tomorrow morning on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we took into consideration that your submission was that to get a visa, it would take five working days. So please, let us know no later than tomorrow morning what will happen on Friday and on Monday next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Besides the videoconferences, and we appreciate that Defence counsel and Madam Dahuron are prepared to work both next following weekends and during the weeks in taking 92 bis statements in the field. The final question is now how to react to that -- the Defence has already apologised for not living up to their obligations in calling witnesses this week. We had the problem with this not adequate filing of a request for assigning a presiding officer for 92 bis statements. That has nothing to do with that what is enshrined in the guidelines for taking 92 bis statements. And then, in addition, despite of our order how to proceed, we did not even receive a motion requesting the admission of additional witnesses under Rule 73 ter (D). Once again, it took our time that we could -- that we were able to proceed based on a perusal of the list of victims and appendix 1 to the motion by the Defence. Confronted with the question whether or not the time would be ripe for sanctions, I have to give the right or grant the right to be heard to the Prosecution on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no comment at all to make on that. We consider that that's a matter entirely for the Trial Chamber and not for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, it's a right and not a duty to comment on this. We discussed it during the break, and I think we take the Defence by their words. And as we did in the other direction in the past, we leave it at this point in time with a stern warning to live up to all the obligations under the rules in the future, and we will not accept any further delay, save you can justify the delay, and we all know that things can happen that are not foreseeable. But in principle, we have set already the deadlines for the proffers. We have ordered the numbers of witnesses to be called during the next four weeks, and we expect that you fulfill these orders. If not, then unfortunately it will -- it would be necessary to reconsider this issue. One additional point, and it was raised by the Prosecution. May I please hear additional comments from your side when we start the discussion on the hearing of Ms. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask that we go into private Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear comments from the Defence on this issue, that we can decide on all the four documents in one decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have -- the Defence has nothing to add in connection with the document which purportedly bears the signature of Dr. Stakic, other than that which we previously shared with the Court. With the three remaining documents, we continue to stand on our position and our motion that they should be excluded and stricken from the record for the reasons given in our written submission. In addition, as the Court very well knows, on paragraph, I believe, 27 of the fourth amended indictment, the signator of one of the documents is a person who is identified as a co-perpetrator, co-conspirator in this alleged joint criminal enterprise. How that document does not meet a manual or a computer search and is produced to us, we still do not understand and cannot appreciate. We believe that the document was in fact always present, and that they were aware of that document, used that document in other proceedings before the Tribunal against other defendants who are allegedly co-conspirators in this theory of joint criminal enterprise and only were given this document during the Defence case for strategic purposes. We believe that that has caused extreme prejudice to the Defence. And leaving the document and that testimony and references to those documents would continue to be prejudicial to the Defence. So we would, as we have in our written submission, orally, respectfully the request the Court to strike that testimony and all reference to those documents and to deny the documents from being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I give the judicial hint, in this case limited to this procedural question, of course, for you, it's not only a procedural question, that under our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it might be that only Rule 95 gives the justification for the exclusion of certain evidence. And we have seen nothing on Rule 95 in your motion. The question of whether or not a document has been 65 terred or not is a totally different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Our application, Your Honour, with all due respect, goes to the significant prejudice, and what we believe respectfully nonetheless to the OTP of a practice of withholding documents that are critical. If they are going to allege, as they do in all eight counts of the indictment, that in fact there was this joint criminal enterprise, and they are more specific than that, they identify co-conspirators by name, by title, and they give us that. They have brought forth no evidence on those alleged co-conspirators on this what I consider to be speculative joint criminal enterprise theory, yet during the Defence case conveniently enough their searches produce documents signed allegedly, authored purportedly by one of the joint co-conspirators. That is extremely significant. The Defence needed and requested those documents. Under no argument or scenario would that document not be a document that should have been produced. We continue to maintain those documents should have been produced. They were not produced. They have caused extreme prejudice to the Defence, and we dare say that we can't wait for the opportunity when our experts appear and more documents will somehow be found and presented to them during their cross-examination. Do we have all the documents for the basis of their complaint and indictment? Or do we only have some documents? We believe that if any other documents are produced, in addition to these that we're discussing, that they also be prevented and prohibited from being introduced as evidence. We certainly understand the practice of producing a document which would perhaps impeach a witness or attack his or her credibility. But to produce a document by a third party on an issue that is clearly one that we have debated in these proceedings for months is, in our submission, something and a practice that should not be permitted. And therefore, once again, and I recognise Rule 65 -- I mean Rule 95. Our request goes beyond that. It goes to the spirit and letter of all the rules, and that is to ensure a fair trial to make sure that there is no prejudice. We truly, as we have set forth in our motion, believe that we are proceeding under, by virtue of these documents, a trial by ambush. Surprise tactics that have long ago been rejected, and we don't come into Court and not share or tell your adversaries what the evidence is or is not. We believe those documents fall within that framework. And unfortunately, Rule 95, I believe, the intent of that is that if a party would bring evidence that somehow the adversary would be able to argue it was made not contemporaneous with the time the document states or fraudulent documents or documents under similar such situations. In the instant case, we have a document that has been produced in other cases on theories that the OTP has advocated time and time again that they have never produced a document until two months until the close of the case in essence. We think it is prejudicial. Despite Rule 95, we believe that prejudice and a fair trial would be denied Dr. Stakic by the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, although we've said everything that was -- I think needs to be said in our written response, there are two things I really need to raise. Your Honours, had we realised that we still had in our possession a signed document by Dr. Stakic, clearly we would have put that document in for handwriting analysis. But second, there's this: Your Honour, Mr. Ostojic complains that we have been withholding documents. Your Honour, we've offered Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Lukic the opportunity to inspect every single document, all hundreds and thousands, under provisions of Rule 66 (B). They declined the opportunity. And may I say, I'm not surprised apart from them having to give us the documents. Your Honour, it is one of those things that with so many documents relating to this particular area, the Prosecution had to make a selection of the ones that they considered relevant to prove their case. If the Defence then call a witness who raises something that wasn't foreseen, for example, that they were going to be concentrating on the dismissals from the military, well then I'm afraid, Your Honour, it would be failing in our duty were we not to bring before Your Honours and the Court those documents which show that that testimony can in some way be undermined. It is not ambush. Ambush is when we deliberately withhold Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents that we know will implicate the defendant in the offences. We didn't know what witnesses were going to be called. We didn't actually know what most of them were going to say even just before they were going to say it. And so, Your Honour, this is under no circumstances an ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We will decide as soon as possible and practical. Before closing today's session, one question: As to the fact that we have lost now effectively two additional days, my question is for both parties: Would there be any obstacle to have once again in deviation from the scheduling order a hearing on Friday, the 7th of March? Taking into account that we still have 15, 1-5, live witnesses before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask Madam Registrar to find out whether there is a possibility to continue with the hearing on Friday, the 7th of March. Then finally, it is -- I regard it as my duty, due to the complaints made by Defence counsel, may I ask Dr. Stakic in person, are there still any complaints in relation to the Detention Unit, in relation to the problems bringing you to the Tribunal and bringing you back, and especially the question, as I read out previously, that it was granted by the United Nations Detention Unit that whenever you request, and coming late back to the Detention Unit, that the mandatory hour of fresh air would be granted to you, and a hot meal would be granted to you on request? Are there any ongoing problems?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did not work last week, and it was a welcome decision because I could have a rest. So it seems to confirm that I was simply too tired and that that was the reason. After five or six days, a doctor came, a doctor of the Detention Unit, came to pay me a visit. And also one of the officers in the prison administration informed me that I was entitled to exercise that right. That is, to have my fresh air outside the usual hours, so that at this particular moment, I really have no other complaints. I'm sorry. As for the transportation, I believe that it happened only that day, and it is simply things like that can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these comments, Dr. Stakic. And if there is no other issue to be dealt with today, then this concludes today's hearing. And the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.
